extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato / readers interested in education, poetry, and moral formation
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Plato's prescriptive criteria for what poets, musicians, and educators may present to the guardian-class in the ideal city (content, style, music, rhythm, instruments, and pedagogical timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit humiliating or shameful depictions of gods and heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not depict gods, demigods, or heroes in states of shame, excessive grief, cowardice, lust, or irreverent behaviour (e.g., gods lamenting, Achilles weeping and wailing, gods saying 'Alas! my misery!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and anti-patterns enumerated: Achilles 'first lying on his side, then on his back, and then on his face', taking sooty ashes and pouring them over his head; Priam 'rolling in the dirt, calling each man loudly by his name.' Such representations should be refused because youth might imitate or accept these unworthy representations of divinity and heroism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid representing the gods as authors of evil or moral failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow poets to portray the gods as the originators of evil or as responsible for base or impious acts (e.g., tales that make heroes or gods commit rape or other dreadful deeds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either the poet must deny that the acts occurred or deny the divine parentage of those who commit them; both together are unacceptable. Rationale: such tales engender lax morals and lead listeners to excuse their own vices by citing divine precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict portrayals that show wicked men prospering
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent poets/storytellers from asserting or implying that wicked men are often happy while the good are miserable, or that injustice is profitable when undetected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These messages are to be forbidden and the opposite taught, because the moral education of the guardians requires presenting justice as advantageous and vice as harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness as a general rule; authorized lying only for rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth should be highly valued; lying is generally useless to the gods and only a 'medicine' for men. If lying is permitted, it is a privilege of rulers for the public good; private individuals must not lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison: like physicians who use medicine, rulers may lie for the public good; anyone else lying is 'equally subversive and destructive' and should be punished, e.g., craftsmen, priests, physicians, carpenters. If a ruler catches others lying, he will punish them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians must not be given to excessive laughter or displays of weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should not be portrayed (nor themselves be) overcome by laughter or trivial lamentation; excessive laughter produces a violent reaction and undermines temperance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban imitative passages that show persons of worth laughing immoderately or gods 'Inextinguishable laughter' at Hephaestus; such depictions are unworthy and injurious to youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote temperance: obedience and self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance for guardians consists chiefly in obedience to commanders and self-control in sensual pleasures; cultural materials must support these elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject verses or tales that praise drunkenness, indulgence, or idleness (e.g., lines extolling cups of wine, or 'O heavy with wine'). Songs and stories should not encourage appetite for drink or sensual excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid depictions that praise love of money or gift-driven behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not sing or narrate stories that celebrate gifts persuading gods/kings or that portray heroes as lovers of money (e.g., advising Achilles to accept gifts, or depicting him as avaricious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Phoenix's counsel to Achilles about taking gifts, or narratives that excuse returning heroic acts only if paid. Such sentiments are 'not sentiments which can be approved.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the kinds of characters guardians may imitate
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians should imitate only virtuous characters (courageous, temperate, holy, free) and should not be trained to imitate women quarrelling, sick, in love, in labour, slaves, craftsmen, sailors, madmen, or other low or base types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: repeated imitation from youth grows into habit and 'a second nature.' Anti-patterns include imitating domestic quarrels, drunken mockery, slavish labour, animal noises, or mad behaviour—these corrupt character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple narration over extensive mimetic imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, poets should adopt a style in which the poet often speaks in his own person (narration) and only rarely personates others; the truly good man will mostly narrate rather than imitate vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation via Homeric example: difference between the poet speaking in his own voice and taking the person of another (imitation). The guardians' ideal speech style is mostly narrative (little imitation), avoiding the pantomimic, many-change style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude pantomimic/multi-role imitative performers from the city
rubrics_metrics.description: Those able to imitate many characters, produce animal sounds, and effect complex mimicry (pantomimic artists) are admired elsewhere but are not permitted to exist in the guardian city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such performers may be garlanded and sent away ceremonially, the law will not allow them to practise in the State because their art trains imitation of all sorts of unsuitable behaviours and sounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict musical modes/harmonies to those expressive of courage and temperance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ban the mixed/tenor Lydian, full-toned/bass Lydian, Ionian, and 'relaxed' harmonies (associated with sorrow, drunkenness, softness, indolence); retain Dorian and Phrygian harmonies for the 'strain of necessity' and the 'strain of freedom'—the warlike and temperate strains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: certain harmonies produce softness and drunkenness, which are 'utterly unbecoming' to guardians. Music must express and habituate courage and temperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit rhythms to those that express noble character; avoid complex metres
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose rhythms that are expressions of a courageous and harmonious life; avoid multiplicity and complex metrical systems and seek rhythms aligned with noble temper rather than novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult specialists (e.g., Damon) to identify which rhythms express meanness, insolence, fury, or their opposites. Simplicity of rhythm aligns with simplicity and nobility of soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict instruments: allow only lyre and harp (and shepherd's pipe in country)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not maintain artificers of many-stringed, 'panharmonic' instruments or makers of complex scales; exclude flute-makers/players from the city; permit only lyre and harp within the city (shepherds may use pipe in countryside).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: panharmonic music and flute are associated with composite, relaxing styles; the lyre and harp align with the simpler, warlike/temperate musical aims of the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical training as primary formative instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical education (words, melody, rhythm) is a potent instrument that fixes rhythm and harmony in the soul and shapes disposition; it must be used to habituate recognition of virtue and disdain for vice from early years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with learning letters: guardians must learn fundamental forms of temperance, courage, liberality, magnificence, and their opposites in all combinations, so they can recognize them everywhere. Musical training makes the soul graceful or ungraceful and enables early moral taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin gymnastic training early and continue through life
rubrics_metrics.description: Gymnastics (physical training) should begin in early years and be sustained through life; bodily training complements musical/political education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's belief: the good soul improves the body as far as possible; gymnastic is the next ordered part after music in guardian education.
